title: Inna and Its Sisters — Completing the Set (لَيْتَ)

steps.title: Four more sisters, one familiar rule
body: You already know إِنَّ, أَنَّ, and لِأَنَّ all push the noun right after them to accusative, leaving the predicate nominative. Four more sisters share that exact rule — new meanings, not a new pattern to learn. كَأَنَّ ("as if") makes a comparison: كَأَنَّ الطَّقْسَ بَارِدٌ الْيَوْمَ — "it's as if the weather is cold today."

لٰكِنَّ is the HEAVY "but" — a real sister of إنّ, unlike the light لَكِنْ you already know (no shadda, no case shift at all): الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ لٰكِنَّ الْحَدِيقَةَ صَغِيرَةٌ — "the house is big, but the garden is small." لَعَلَّ ("perhaps") expresses hope or expectation: لَعَلَّ الطَّقْسَ جَمِيلٌ غَدًا — "perhaps the weather will be beautiful tomorrow."

لَيْتَ ("would that / I wish") is different from an ordinary hope — it marks an irrealis wish, usually for something unlikely or impossible: لَيْتَ الطَّقْسَ دَافِئٌ — "would that the weather were warm," said precisely because it probably isn't. That completes all ten traditionally-listed sisters by name. Only their attached-pronoun forms (إِنَّهُ, أَنَّهَا, …) are still ahead.

steps.title: The last four sisters
steps.intro: Read each sentence and check the noun's ending right after the sister of إنّ. Tap 🔊 to hear any line.

steps.title: As if
steps.prompt: What does كَأَنَّ add to this sentence?
steps.explanation: كَأَنَّ makes a comparison or simile, and — like every sister of إنّ — pushes الطَّقْسَ to accusative right after it.

steps.title: Heavy vs. light "but"
steps.prompt: Why is الْحَدِيقَةَ accusative here, when the same word after لَكِنْ (no shadda) would stay nominative?

options.label: لٰكِنَّ (with shadda) is a sister of إِنَّ and shifts case; لَكِنْ is a completely different, lighter word that doesn't
لٰكِنَّ and لَكِنْ are the same word, just spelled two ways
Every noun after "but" is always accusative in Arabic

steps.explanation: لٰكِنَّ (heavy, doubled ن) is one of the ten sisters of إنّ; لَكِنْ (light, single ن) is an unrelated, more common word that never shifts case. Only the heavy form does this.

steps.title: A real wish, not a request
steps.prompt: How is لَيْتَ different from لَعَلَّ ("perhaps")?

options.label: لَيْتَ marks a wish for something unlikely or impossible; لَعَلَّ is a more realistic hope or expectation
They mean exactly the same thing and can always replace each other
لَيْتَ is used only in questions

steps.explanation: لَيْتَ is an irrealis wish — you say it precisely because the thing probably isn't true. لَعَلَّ instead expresses something you genuinely think might happen.

steps.title: All ten sisters, named
steps.message: كَأَنَّ, لٰكِنَّ, لَعَلَّ, and لَيْتَ complete the ten traditionally-listed sisters of إنّ — every one of them pushing the following noun to accusative, the same rule you first met with إِنَّ. Their attached-pronoun forms are still ahead.
